slides.narration: Welcome. When atoms are heated or excited by electricity they give out light, and the pattern of colours is different for every element. In this part we look at the different kinds of spectrum, then at Niels Bohr’s idea that electrons occupy fixed energy levels, which explained the spectrum of hydrogen so well.

slides.heading: Emission and absorption spectra
slides.body_md: An **emission spectrum** is the light given out by excited atoms: **bright lines on a dark background**. An **absorption spectrum** forms when white light passes through a cool gas: **dark lines on a bright continuous background**. For one element the dark lines fall at **the same wavelengths** as its bright lines.

rows: Excite atoms by heat or electricity
Pass white light through cool gas
Find elements in stars and cool gas clouds

visual.alt: Table comparing emission and absorption spectra

slides.narration: An emission spectrum is what you see when excited atoms give out light: a few bright lines on a dark background. An absorption spectrum is made by passing white light through a cool gas. The gas takes out certain colours and leaves dark lines. The dark lines of an element sit at exactly the same places as its bright lines.

slides.heading: Line spectra and band spectra
slides.body_md: A **line spectrum** is made of sharp lines at definite wavelengths, produced by **excited atoms**. A **band spectrum** is made of groups of closely spaced lines that merge into bands, produced by **excited molecules**. A hot solid gives a **continuous spectrum**.

rows: Bands, sharp edge on one side

visual.alt: Table of continuous, line and band spectra with sources

slides.narration: There are three kinds of spectrum to know. A hot solid, like a bulb filament, gives a continuous spectrum with every colour. Excited atoms give sharp separate lines. Excited molecules give groups of lines so close together that they look like bands. Molecules have many closely spaced energy levels, which is why their lines crowd together.

slides.heading: The four spectra side by side
slides.body_md: Compare the strips. The **hydrogen emission lines** and the **hydrogen absorption lines** are at identical wavelengths (410, 434, 486 and 656 nm). The band spectrum is made of crowded lines.

slides.heading: Why atoms give lines
slides.body_md: The electron in an atom can have only **certain energies (energy levels)**. Light is emitted or absorbed only when the electron changes level, as one **photon** with $\Delta E = h\nu$. Only certain gaps exist, so only **certain wavelengths** appear.

nodes.label: Atom absorbs energy; electron goes to a higher level
Electron falls to a lower level
One photon leaves: ΔE = hν, giving one spectral line

visual.alt: Flow chart: an electron is excited, falls back and emits one photon whose energy is the gap between two levels

slides.narration: Why lines and not a smooth band of colours? Because the electron in an atom is allowed only certain energies. When the atom is excited the electron moves up. When it falls back, the energy difference leaves as a single photon. Since only certain gaps exist, only certain wavelengths are emitted, and each element has its own set of gaps.

slides.heading: Bohr’s postulates
slides.body_md: **1.** The electron moves in certain circular **stationary orbits** and does **not radiate** in them. **2.** An orbit is allowed only if the angular momentum is $m v r = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, $n = 1, 2, 3\ldots$ **3.** Energy is emitted or absorbed only in a **jump** between orbits, $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = h\nu$.

visual.alt: Table of the three postulates of Bohr’s model and what each explains

slides.narration: Bohr made three postulates. First, the electron moves only in certain circular orbits, called stationary orbits, and does not radiate energy while in one. Second, the angular momentum in an allowed orbit is a whole number times Planck’s constant divided by two pi. Third, light is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits.

slides.heading: Bohr orbits drawn to scale
slides.body_md: For $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$ the radii are in the ratio $1 : 4 : 9 : 16$ because $r \propto n^2$. For He⁺ every orbit is **half** the size of the matching hydrogen orbit because the nuclear charge is twice as large.

slides.narration: Here are the orbits for hydrogen on the left and for the helium plus ion on the right. The radius grows as n squared, so the outer orbits are far apart. In helium plus the nucleus has twice the charge and pulls the electron in, so each orbit has half the radius of the hydrogen orbit with the same n.

slides.heading: Radius, speed and energy: numericals only
slides.body_md: For a **hydrogen-like** species (one electron, nuclear charge $Z$) in the $n$th orbit use the given results; **no derivation** is needed. $$r_n = \frac{52.9\,n^2}{Z}\ \text{pm}, \quad v_n = 2.18 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{Z}{n}\ \text{m s}^{-1}, \quad E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\frac{Z^2}{n^2}\ \text{J}$$ The energy is negative: the bound electron has less energy than a free one (zero at $n = \infty$).

visual.alt: Table showing how radius, speed and energy depend on n and Z

slides.narration: You do not need to derive these formulas, only to use them. The radius is fifty-two point nine picometres times n squared, divided by the nuclear charge. The speed is two point one eight million metres per second times Z over n. The energy is negative, because the bound electron has less energy than a free electron, which has zero.

slides.heading: Worked example: orbit of an He⁺ ion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The electron of an $\ce{He+}$ ion ($Z = 2$) is in the fourth orbit. Find its radius, speed and energy.

**Radius:** $r_4 = \dfrac{52.9 \times 4^2}{2} = 423.2$ pm.

**Speed:** $v_4 = 2.18 \times 10^{6} \times \dfrac{2}{4} = 1.09 \times 10^{6}$ m s⁻¹.

**Energy:** $E_4 = -2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times \dfrac{2^2}{4^2} = -5.45 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

visual.alt: Table of the radius, speed and energy of He plus in the fourth orbit

slides.narration: Substitute Z equal to two and n equal to four into each formula. The radius is about four hundred twenty-three picometres, eight times the first Bohr radius. The speed is half that of the ground-state electron in hydrogen, about one point zero nine million metres per second. The energy is small and negative, as for any bound level.

slides.body_md: Substitute n and Z into the radius formula.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use the radius formula with the numbers given in the question. Be careful to square the value of n, not to cube it or multiply it by itself only once, and remember that the nuclear charge Z goes in the denominator, so a larger charge gives a smaller orbit.

slides.heading: Energy changes and ionisation
slides.body_md: The energy absorbed in a jump is the **difference** of the two levels; the **ionisation energy** is the energy to lift the electron from $n$ to $n = \infty$. For hydrogen in its ground state it is $2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J per atom, which is **1312 kJ mol⁻¹**. For hydrogen-like ions it is multiplied by $Z^2$.

visual.alt: Table of ionisation energies of H, He plus and Li two plus from the ground state

slides.narration: The energy absorbed in a jump is the difference between the two levels. The ionisation energy is the energy needed to lift the electron from its level to infinity, where its energy is zero. For ground-state hydrogen this is two point one eight times ten to the minus eighteen joule. For hydrogen-like ions it is multiplied by Z squared.

slides.heading: Worked example: excitation and ionisation of hydrogen
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) Find the energy absorbed when the electron of a hydrogen atom goes from $n = 1$ to $n = 4$, and the wavelength of the photon absorbed. (b) Find the ionisation energy per mole. ($N_\text{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)

**(a)** $\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{16}\right) = 2.04 \times 10^{-18}$ J; $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{2.04 \times 10^{-18}} = 97.3 \times 10^{-9}$ m $= 97.3$ nm.

**(b)** $2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.31 \times 10^{6}$ J mol⁻¹, i.e. about 1313 kJ mol⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the results of the excitation and ionisation example

slides.narration: Work out the energy difference between the two levels, then divide Planck’s constant times the speed of light by it to find the wavelength of the photon that must be absorbed. It lies in the ultraviolet. For the ionisation energy per mole, multiply the energy for one atom by Avogadro’s number, giving about thirteen hundred kilojoules.

slides.heading: Merits of Bohr’s model
slides.body_md: Bohr’s model **explained the stability** of the atom, **explained the line spectrum of hydrogen** (it gives the Rydberg formula), and gave the **radii and energies** of one-electron species such as He⁺, Li²⁺ and Be³⁺. It introduced **quantisation of energy** into atomic structure.

rows: Same formulas with Z in place

visual.alt: Table of the successes of Bohr’s model

slides.narration: Here is what Bohr’s model achieved. It explained why the atom is stable, with orbits in which no radiation occurs. It explained the line spectrum of hydrogen as jumps between levels, and gave the right ionisation energy. It also worked for ions with a single electron, such as helium plus, simply by putting in the right nuclear charge.

slides.body_md: Use the radius formula with the larger nuclear charge.
slides.narration: Quick check. The ion has a single electron, so the formula applies directly. Substitute the nuclear charge and the orbit number, and compare your answer with the hydrogen value of two hundred twelve picometres for the second orbit, since a larger charge should give a smaller orbit.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Emission spectra have bright lines and absorption spectra have dark lines at the same places. Atoms give lines and molecules give bands. Bohr proposed stationary orbits with quantised angular momentum, and light from jumps between them. His model gives the radius, speed and energy for hydrogen and one-electron ions.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 2. First we use the energy levels of hydrogen to understand its series of spectral lines and calculate their wavelengths. slides.heading: Series of lines in the hydrogen spectrum
slides.body_md: Each series is the set of lines for electrons falling to **one lower level $n_1$** from higher levels. The series are named **Lyman** ($n_1 = 1$), **Balmer** ($n_1 = 2$), **Paschen** (3), **Brackett** (4) and **Pfund** (5).

visual.alt: Table of the hydrogen series, lower level, region and wavelength of the first line

slides.narration: The lines of hydrogen fall into series. Each series contains the lines made when an electron falls to the same lower level. The Lyman series ends on the first level and lies in the ultraviolet. The Balmer series ends on the second level and is visible. Paschen, Brackett and Pfund lie in the infrared.

slides.heading: Energy levels and the series
slides.body_md: The longest line of each series comes from the **smallest gap** (to the next level above) and the **series limit** from the gap to $n = \infty$. Levels **crowd together** as $n$ increases.

visual.caption: E = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J / n².

slides.narration: This diagram is drawn to scale. Blue arrows ending on the first level make the Lyman series, red arrows ending on the second make the Balmer series, and brown arrows ending on the third make the Paschen series. The levels crowd together at the top, so lines in each series bunch together towards a limit at short wavelength.

slides.heading: The Rydberg formula
slides.body_md: The wave number of a line is $$\bar{\nu} = \frac{1}{\lambda} = R_\text{H}\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right), \qquad R_\text{H} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1},\ n_2 > n_1$$ **Longest wavelength** of a series: $n_2 = n_1 + 1$. **Series limit** (shortest): $n_2 = \infty$.

visual.alt: Table of the longest wavelength and the series limit for the Lyman, Balmer and Paschen series

slides.narration: Rydberg’s formula gives the reciprocal of the wavelength as a constant times the difference of two terms, one for each level. The constant is one point zero nine seven times ten to the seventh per metre. The longest line in a series has n two equal to n one plus one, and the series limit has n two at infinity.

slides.heading: Worked example: a Balmer line
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the wavelength of the line emitted when the electron falls from $n = 6$ to $n = 2$ in hydrogen. ($R_\text{H} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$)

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{36}\right) = 2.44 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2.44 \times 10^{6}} = 4.10 \times 10^{-7}$ m $= 410.2$ nm: violet light of the Balmer series.

visual.alt: Table of the results of the Balmer line example

slides.narration: Put n one equal to two and n two equal to six into the Rydberg formula. The bracket is a quarter minus one thirty-sixth. That gives the wave number, and taking the reciprocal gives the wavelength, about four hundred ten nanometres. This is the violet line of the Balmer series, close to the series limit.

slides.heading: Quick check: Rydberg calculation
slides.body_md: Evaluate the bracket first, then take the reciprocal.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the two levels into the Rydberg formula, work out the fractions in the bracket, multiply by the Rydberg constant, and then take the reciprocal. Finally convert metres to nanometres by multiplying by one billion, and check that your answer lies in the visible region for a Balmer line.

slides.heading: Defects of Bohr’s model
slides.body_md: Bohr’s model **fails for atoms with more than one electron**, cannot explain the **splitting of lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) or an electric field (Stark effect)**, and treats the electron as a **particle in a definite orbit**, ignoring its wave nature and conflicting with the **uncertainty principle**.

rows: One quantum number is not enough

visual.alt: Table of the defects of Bohr’s model with the reason for each

slides.narration: Bohr’s model has important defects. It works only for atoms with one electron, because it ignores repulsion between electrons. It cannot explain how spectral lines split in magnetic and electric fields. And it pictures the electron as a particle on a path of known radius, which conflicts with the wave nature of matter and with the uncertainty principle.

slides.heading: Quick check: what Bohr could not explain
slides.body_md: Pick the observation that lies outside Bohr’s model.
slides.narration: Quick check. Three of the four options are explained by the model: the line spectrum of hydrogen, the spectrum of a one-electron ion, and the stability of the atom. Decide which observation would need more than one quantum number, or a more advanced theory, and choose that option.

slides.heading: Dual nature and de Broglie’s relation
slides.body_md: Light shows both wave and particle behaviour. In 1924 de Broglie suggested that **matter too has wave properties**: a particle of mass $m$ and speed $v$ has the wavelength $$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{p}$$ The wavelength is **measurable for electrons** and **negligible for large objects**.

visual.alt: Table of de Broglie wavelengths of an electron, an alpha particle and a car

slides.narration: De Broglie suggested that if light can act as a particle, matter can act as a wave. A particle of mass m and speed v has a wavelength equal to Planck’s constant divided by its momentum. For an electron this is comparable with the size of an atom. For a car it is so tiny that no experiment could ever detect it.

slides.heading: Standing electron waves in an orbit
slides.body_md: An orbit is allowed if a **whole number of wavelengths** fits its circumference, $2\pi r = n\lambda$; otherwise the wave cancels itself. With $\lambda = h/mv$ this gives **Bohr’s quantum condition** $mvr = nh/2\pi$.

visual.alt: An electron wave with three whole wavelengths round an orbit joins up and is allowed, while a wave with three and a half wavelengths does not join and is not allowed
visual.caption: Circumference = a whole number of wavelengths.

slides.narration: De Broglie waves give a picture of Bohr’s rule. On the left a wave with exactly three wavelengths round the orbit joins up with itself, so it can persist, and the orbit is allowed. On the right, three and a half wavelengths do not join up and the wave destroys itself, so such an orbit cannot exist.

slides.heading: Worked example: de Broglie wavelengths
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the de Broglie wavelength of (a) an electron moving at $1.5 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and (b) a car of mass $1500$ kg moving at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$)

**(a)** $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_\text{e}v} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.5 \times 10^{6}} = 4.85 \times 10^{-10}$ m $= 485$ pm.

**(b)** $\lambda = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{1500 \times 20} = 2.21 \times 10^{-38}$ m.

visual.alt: Table of the wavelengths for the electron and the car and whether they are observable

slides.narration: Substitute into lambda equal to h over m v. For the electron the wavelength is about four hundred eighty-five picometres, which is about twice the diameter of an atom, so electron waves can be diffracted by crystals. For the car the wavelength is about ten to the minus thirty-eight metres, far smaller than anything measurable.

slides.heading: Quick check: a moving ball
slides.body_md: Convert the mass to kilograms before using $\lambda = h/mv$.
slides.narration: Quick check. Convert the mass of the ball from grams to kilograms first. Then divide Planck’s constant by the product of mass and speed. Expect an extremely small answer, because the mass of an everyday object is enormous compared with the mass of an electron. Give the result in the units asked for.

slides.heading: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle
slides.body_md: It is **impossible to know exactly and at the same time both the position and the momentum** of a microscopic particle. $$\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq \frac{h}{4\pi}, \qquad \Delta p = m\,\Delta v$$ A **smaller $\Delta x$** means a **larger $\Delta v$**. The effect is **negligible for large objects**.

nodes.label: Fix the position of an electron more precisely
Δp must become larger, Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π

visual.alt: Flow chart of the uncertainty principle: a smaller uncertainty in position forces a larger uncertainty in momentum

slides.narration: Heisenberg showed that nature sets a limit to how well we can know the position and momentum of a tiny particle together. The product of the two uncertainties is at least Planck’s constant divided by four pi. If you pin down the position more tightly, the momentum becomes less certain. For large objects the limit is far too small to matter.

slides.heading: Worked example: uncertainty in speed
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) The position of an electron is known to within $1.0 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{m}$. Find the minimum uncertainty in its speed. (b) Do the same for a marble of mass $1.0$ g whose position is known to within $1.0$ mm. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)

**(a)** $\Delta v = \dfrac{h}{4\pi m_\text{e}\Delta x} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{4 \times \pi \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-9}} = 5.79 \times 10^{4}$ m s⁻¹.

**(b)** $\Delta v = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{4 \times \pi \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 5.27 \times 10^{-29}$ m s⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the minimum uncertainty in speed for an electron and a marble

slides.narration: Rearrange the principle to give the uncertainty in speed as Planck’s constant divided by four pi times the mass times the uncertainty in position. For the electron the uncertainty in speed is about fifty-eight thousand metres per second, which is huge. For the marble it is about five times ten to the minus twenty-nine metres per second, which is totally negligible.

slides.heading: From orbits to orbitals
slides.body_md: Because position and momentum cannot both be known, the **definite orbit** of Bohr must be replaced by a region where the electron is **most probably found**. This leads to the **orbital** of the quantum mechanical model, with a wave function that describes the electron as a matter wave.

rows: Electron in a fixed circular orbit
Electron described by a wave; probability of being found

visual.alt: Table comparing Bohr’s orbit picture with the wave mechanical picture

slides.narration: The uncertainty principle means a definite path for the electron has no meaning. Instead, the electron is described by a wave, and we can only say where it is likely to be found. The Bohr orbit is replaced by a region of high probability called an orbital. This opens the way to the quantum mechanical model of the atom.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Series: Lyman (n₁ = 1, UV), Balmer (2, visible), Paschen (3, IR), Brackett (4), Pfund (5).
Defects of Bohr’s model: many-electron atoms, Zeeman and Stark effects, particle picture against uncertainty principle.
de Broglie: λ = h/mv. Heisenberg: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π.

visual.alt: Summary table of the main formulae of Part 2

slides.narration: Summing up Part 2. Hydrogen lines fall into series named by the lower level, and the Rydberg formula gives their wavelengths. Bohr’s model works for one-electron species but has important defects. De Broglie showed that moving matter has a wavelength equal to Planck’s constant over momentum. Heisenberg showed that position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2

Longest wavelength: n₂ = n₁ + 1. Shortest wavelength (series limit): n₂ = ∞.

In uncertainty numericals use Δp = mΔv and the form h/4π.
For a large object the wavelength or uncertainty comes out immeasurably small: say so.

Mass in grams in λ = h/mv

sections.heading: 1. Emission and absorption spectra; line and band spectra
sections.body_md:
An **emission spectrum** is the radiation given out by excited atoms or molecules; an **absorption spectrum** is obtained when white light passes through a cool gas and certain wavelengths are removed. For one substance the dark absorption lines and the bright emission lines are at the **same wavelengths**.

A **continuous spectrum** (hot solids, the Sun) has all wavelengths without a break. A **line spectrum** has sharp lines at definite wavelengths and is produced by **atoms**; a **band spectrum** has groups of closely spaced lines forming bands and is produced by **molecules**. Because each element has its own set of lines, a line spectrum identifies the element.

key_terms.definition_md: The spectrum of light given out by atoms or molecules that have been excited.
A continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines at wavelengths absorbed by a cool gas.
A spectrum of sharp lines at definite wavelengths, produced by atoms.
A spectrum of groups of closely spaced lines that merge into bands, produced by molecules.

sections.heading: 2. Bohr’s postulates and merits
sections.body_md:
**Postulates:** (1) The electron moves in certain circular **stationary orbits** and does not radiate in them. (2) The angular momentum in an allowed orbit is a whole-number multiple of $h/2\pi$: $m v r = nh/2\pi$. (3) Energy is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits: $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = h\nu$.

**Merits:** explains the stability of the atom; explains the line spectrum of hydrogen (and gives the Rydberg formula); gives radii, speeds and energies for one-electron species H, He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺; introduced the quantisation of energy.

key_terms.definition_md: An allowed orbit in which the electron has fixed energy and does not radiate.

sections.heading: 3. Radius, speed and energy of the nth orbit (numericals; no derivation)
sections.body_md:
The derivation of these expressions is **not required**. For a species with one electron and nuclear charge $Z$ in the $n$th orbit:

$r_n = 52.9\,n^2/Z$ pm; $v_n = 2.18 \times 10^{6}\,Z/n$ m s⁻¹; $E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,Z^2/n^2$ J. The energy is negative (zero when $n = \infty$). The **ionisation energy** from level $n$ is $2.18 \times 10^{-18} Z^2/n^2$ J per ion; for ground-state hydrogen it is 1312 kJ mol⁻¹. The energy of a jump is $\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} Z^2 (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2)$ J.

key_terms.definition_md: An atom or ion with a single electron, such as H, He⁺, Li²⁺ or Be³⁺.
The energy needed to remove an electron completely from the atom or ion in a given level.

sections.heading: 4. Hydrogen spectrum and the Rydberg formula
sections.body_md:
Hydrogen lines form **series**, named by the lower level $n_1$: **Lyman** ($n_1 = 1$, ultraviolet), **Balmer** (2, visible), **Paschen** (3, infrared), **Brackett** (4, infrared), **Pfund** (5, infrared). The Rydberg formula is $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_\text{H}\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$, $n_2 > n_1$, $R_\text{H} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$.

The **longest wavelength** of a series has $n_2 = n_1 + 1$; the **series limit** (shortest) has $n_2 = \infty$. From $n$ to the ground state an atom can give $n(n-1)/2$ different lines by all possible routes.

key_terms.definition_md: The shortest wavelength of a series, produced by a fall from n = ∞.
The reciprocal of the wavelength, 1/λ, in m⁻¹.

sections.heading: 5. Defects of Bohr’s model
sections.body_md: (1) It applies only to **one-electron species**; it ignores electron–electron repulsion and fails for He and other atoms. (2) It cannot explain the **splitting of spectral lines** in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) or in an electric field (Stark effect). (3) It treats the electron as a **particle in a definite orbit**, ignoring its **wave nature** and contradicting **Heisenberg's uncertainty principle**. (4) It does not explain how atoms form chemical bonds.

key_terms.definition_md: Splitting of spectral lines when the source is placed in a magnetic field.
Splitting of spectral lines when the source is placed in an electric field.

rows: Conflicts with uncertainty principle and wave nature

sections.heading: 6. Dual nature of matter and de Broglie’s equation
sections.body_md: Radiation shows both wave and particle behaviour. **de Broglie (1924):** every moving particle has an associated wave of wavelength $\lambda = h/mv = h/p$. For an electron $\lambda$ is about $10^{-10}$ m, so electrons are diffracted by crystals; for a ball $\lambda$ is about $10^{-34}$ m and cannot be observed. In a Bohr orbit, a **whole number of wavelengths** fits the circumference, $2\pi r = n\lambda$, which gives $m v r = nh/2\pi$.

key_terms.definition_md: The wave associated with a moving particle, of wavelength λ = h/mv.
The product of mass and velocity, p = mv.

visual.alt: An electron wave with three whole wavelengths round an orbit joins up and is allowed, while a wave with three and a half wavelengths does not join and is not allowed
visual.caption: Circumference = a whole number of wavelengths.

sections.heading: 7. Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle
sections.body_md: It is impossible to measure **both the position and the momentum** of a microscopic particle exactly at the same time: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq h/4\pi$, with $\Delta p = m\,\Delta v$. The more exactly the position is fixed (small $\Delta x$), the less exactly the speed is known (large $\Delta v$). For an electron in an atom this is significant; for a large object it is negligible. The principle shows that a **definite orbit** has no meaning and leads to the idea of an **orbital**, a region of high probability.

key_terms.definition_md: The statement that the position and momentum of a microscopic particle cannot both be known exactly: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π.
A region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is high.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing a positive energy for a bound electron; the energy of every Bohr level is negative.
- Using Bohr's formulas for species with more than one electron.
- Forgetting to square n in the radius formula, or to divide by Z.
- Using n₂ = n₁ for the first line of a series (it is n₁ + 1), or confusing the series limit with the first line.
- Forgetting to convert grams to kilograms or nanometres to metres.
- Leaving out the 4π in the uncertainty principle.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Postulates of Bohr's theory: one mark each.
- Radius, speed and energy numericals: formula, substitution with n and Z, answer with units.
- Rydberg formula numericals: bracket evaluated, reciprocal, conversion to nm, region named.
- de Broglie and uncertainty numericals: formula, SI units, result, and a one-line comment on size.

questions.stem_md: A student sprinkles a pinch of lithium chloride on a Bunsen flame and views the flame through a hand spectroscope. She sees:

options.text_md: a continuous band of all colours from violet to red
a few bright coloured lines on a dark background
dark lines crossing a bright continuous background
a single dark band in the middle of the field

questions.solution_md: Excited lithium atoms emit light only at certain wavelengths, so the emission spectrum is a few bright lines — option (b).

questions.stem_md: White light from a lamp is passed through a tube of cool hydrogen gas and then through a prism. The spectrum observed is:

options.text_md: a few bright lines on a dark background
a continuous spectrum with no gaps in it
groups of closely spaced bright lines forming bands
a continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines at the wavelengths that hydrogen emits

questions.solution_md: The cool gas absorbs exactly the wavelengths it would emit, giving dark lines in the continuous spectrum — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A discharge tube holding nitrogen gas gives groups of closely spaced lines, each group ending sharply on one side. This kind of spectrum is a:

options.text_md: line emission spectrum, produced by excited atoms
band emission spectrum, produced by excited molecules
continuous spectrum, produced by a hot solid
line absorption spectrum, produced by cool atoms

questions.solution_md: Molecules have many closely spaced energy changes, so their lines crowd into bands — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Three lamps are viewed through a spectroscope. Lamp X shows an unbroken band of colours, lamp Y shows only a few sharp bright lines, and lamp Z shows groups of closely spaced lines. Which identification is most likely?

options.text_md: X is a sodium vapour lamp, Y is a tungsten filament bulb and Z is a tube of nitrogen gas
X is a tungsten filament bulb, Y is a sodium vapour lamp and Z is a tube of nitrogen gas
X is a tube of nitrogen gas, Y is a tungsten filament bulb and Z is a sodium vapour lamp
X is a tungsten filament bulb, Y is a tube of nitrogen gas and Z is a sodium vapour lamp

questions.solution_md: A hot solid gives a continuous spectrum (X), atoms give a few sharp lines (Y, sodium vapour) and molecules give bands of closely spaced lines (Z, nitrogen) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: An astronomer finds dark lines in the spectrum of starlight at exactly the wavelengths of the bright lines that helium emits in the laboratory. This shows that:

options.text_md: the star is made of helium only
the star is moving towards the Earth at high speed
helium is present in the cooler outer layers of the star, absorbing those wavelengths
the star emits a band spectrum like a molecule

questions.solution_md: An absorption line appears at the same wavelength as the emission line of the same atom, so helium gas absorbs the starlight on its way out — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The dark lines in the absorption spectrum of sodium appear at the same wavelengths as the bright lines in its emission spectrum.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. An atom absorbs the same wavelengths that it can emit, because both correspond to jumps between the same energy levels.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Each element has its own characteristic line emission spectrum.

**Reason (R):** The allowed energy levels of the electrons in an atom are different for different elements.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both true; line positions depend on the energy gaps between levels, which differ from element to element, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: How does an emission spectrum differ from an absorption spectrum? Say how the lines of the two spectra of the same element are related.

answer.model_answer_md: An emission spectrum is the radiation given out by atoms excited by heat or electricity, and it appears as bright lines on a dark background. An absorption spectrum is obtained when white light passes through a cool gas; the gas removes certain wavelengths, leaving dark lines on a continuous bright background. For a given element the dark lines occur at the same wavelengths as its bright lines.

questions.stem_md: Why do excited atoms give sharp line spectra while excited molecules such as those of nitrogen usually give band spectra?

answer.model_answer_md: In an atom the electron can change only between a few widely separated energy levels, so only a few definite wavelengths are emitted, giving separate lines. A molecule has, in addition, many closely spaced vibrational and rotational energy levels, so a very large number of closely spaced wavelengths are emitted and the lines merge into groups called bands.

questions.solution_md: Few levels for atoms; many closely spaced levels for molecules.

marking_scheme.step: Atoms: few definite energy changes, lines
Molecules: many closely spaced changes, bands

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a continuous spectrum, a line spectrum and a band spectrum, giving one source of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A continuous spectrum contains all wavelengths of a region without a break, e.g. sunlight or the light of a white-hot filament. A line spectrum consists of separate, sharp lines of definite wavelengths, produced by excited atoms such as those in a sodium vapour lamp or hydrogen discharge tube. A band spectrum consists of groups of closely spaced lines that merge into bands, produced by excited molecules such as nitrogen in a discharge tube.

questions.solution_md: Three kinds of spectrum with a source of each.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe how an emission line spectrum and an absorption line spectrum of hydrogen are obtained. [2]

(b) State how the two spectra of hydrogen are related, and explain what each spectrum shows about the structure of the atom. [2]

(c) Why can the line spectrum of an element be used to identify it? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Emission: hydrogen gas in a discharge tube is excited by a high voltage and its light is analysed with a prism or grating, giving bright lines on a dark background. Absorption: white light is passed through cool hydrogen and then analysed, giving a continuous spectrum with dark lines.

(b) The dark lines occur at the same wavelengths as the bright lines. Both show that the atom has only certain allowed energy levels, and that light is emitted or absorbed only when an electron changes between them.

(c) The set of wavelengths is fixed by the energy levels, which are different for each element, so the pattern is characteristic, like a fingerprint.

questions.solution_md: Two spectra; same positions and quantised levels; fingerprint.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a postulate of Bohr’s theory of the hydrogen atom?

options.text_md: The angular momentum of the electron in a stationary orbit is a whole-number multiple of h/2π
The electron may possess any energy while circling the nucleus
An electron in a stationary orbit radiates energy continuously
The energy of an orbit rises as its radius decreases

questions.solution_md: Bohr quantised the angular momentum: m v r = n h/2π, with n = 1, 2, 3 … — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An electron in the n = 3 orbit of a hydrogen atom does not radiate energy. According to Bohr this is because:

options.text_md: the electron has no kinetic energy in that orbit
the nucleus supplies energy to the electron at the same rate
the orbit is the one nearest to the nucleus
it is in a stationary state of fixed energy, and energy is exchanged only when it jumps between orbits

questions.solution_md: Bohr postulated that an electron in an allowed orbit has fixed energy and does not radiate; radiation appears only in a transition — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The radius of the $n$th Bohr orbit of a hydrogen-like species is $r_n = 52.9\,n^2/Z$ pm. The radius of the third orbit of a hydrogen atom is:

options.text_md: 159 pm
476 pm
53 pm

questions.solution_md: $r_3 = 52.9 \times 3^2 / 1 = 476.1$ pm $\approx 476$ pm — option (b). Options (a) and (d) use $n$ and $n^3$ instead of $n^2$.

questions.stem_md: A beam contains $\ce{Li^2+}$ ions ($Z = 3$) with the electron in the second orbit. Using $r_n = 52.9\,n^2/Z$ pm, the radius of this orbit is:

options.text_md: 106 pm
212 pm

questions.solution_md: $r_2 = 52.9 \times 2^2 / 3 = 70.5$ pm — option (c). The larger nuclear charge pulls the orbit in, so the radius is smaller than the 212 pm of hydrogen.

questions.stem_md: Using $E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,Z^2/n^2$ J, the energy of the electron in the $n = 2$ level of $\ce{He+}$ compared with its energy in the $n = 1$ level of hydrogen is in the ratio:
questions.solution_md: $E(\ce{He+}, n{=}2) = -2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times 4/4 = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J, the same as $E(\text{H}, n{=}1)$, so the ratio is 1 : 1 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a plasma experiment, ground-state $\ce{He+}$ ions are ionised completely. Taking $E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,Z^2/n^2$ J and $N_\text{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, the energy needed per mole of $\ce{He+}$ is closest to:
questions.solution_md: Ionisation energy $= 2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times Z^2 = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times 4 = 8.72 \times 10^{-18}$ J per ion, and per mole $8.72 \times 10^{-18} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} / 1000 = 5250$ kJ — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The radius of the nth Bohr orbit of hydrogen is proportional to n².

**Reason (R):** The energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom becomes less negative as n increases.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the energy trend does not explain the radius law, which follows from quantised angular momentum and the balance of forces — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A beryllium ion $\ce{Be^3+}$ ($Z = 4$) has its single electron in the fourth orbit. Calculate the radius of this orbit in pm, using $r_n = 52.9\,n^2/Z$ pm.
The electron of a $\ce{He+}$ ion in a hot plasma is in the third orbit. Using $v_n = 2.18 \times 10^{6}\,Z/n$ m s⁻¹, calculate its speed in units of $10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
Match each quantity of a hydrogen-like species in the nth orbit with its expression.

options.text_md: Radius
Energy
Speed
Angular momentum

questions.solution_md: Radius → r (52.9 n²/Z); energy → p (−2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ Z²/n²); speed → s (2.18 × 10⁶ Z/n); angular momentum → q (nh/2π).

questions.stem_md: State two merits of Bohr’s model of the hydrogen atom.

answer.model_answer_md: It explained the stability of the atom by proposing stationary orbits in which the electron does not radiate. It explained the line spectrum of hydrogen, and gave the correct wavelengths of the lines (the Rydberg formula), by treating each line as a jump between two energy levels; it also gave the radii and energies of hydrogen-like ions such as He⁺ and Li²⁺.

questions.solution_md: Stability; hydrogen spectrum and hydrogen-like ions.

questions.stem_md: A hydrogen atom in a discharge tube is raised from its ground state to the third level. Using $E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}/n^2$ J, calculate the energy of the electron in the $n = 3$ level and the energy absorbed.
State the three main postulates of Bohr’s theory of the atom.

answer.model_answer_md: First, an electron moves round the nucleus only in certain allowed circular orbits (stationary states), in which it does not radiate energy, each orbit having a definite energy. Second, an orbit is allowed only if the angular momentum of the electron in it is a whole-number multiple of h/2π, m v r = nh/2π. Third, energy is emitted or absorbed only when an electron jumps from one orbit to another, as one photon of energy ΔE = hν equal to the difference between the two energies.

questions.solution_md: Stationary orbits, quantised angular momentum, ΔE = hν.

questions.stem_md: The electron of a $\ce{Be^3+}$ ion ($Z = 4$) is in the second orbit. Using $r_n = 52.9\,n^2/Z$ pm, $v_n = 2.18 \times 10^{6}\,Z/n$ m s⁻¹ and $E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,Z^2/n^2$ J, calculate the radius, the speed and the energy of the electron.

In the second orbit of hydrogen the radius is $211.6$ pm and the speed of the electron is $1.09 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. If the electron wave fits the orbit as a standing wave, find the wavelength from $2\pi r = n\lambda$, find it again from the de Broglie relation, and compare the two. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$)

answer.model_answer_md: From $2\pi r = n\lambda$ with $n = 2$: $\lambda = \dfrac{2 \times 3.1416 \times 211.6}{2} = 664.8$ pm. From de Broglie: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_\text{e}v} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.09 \times 10^{6}} = 6.67 \times 10^{-10}$ m, i.e. about 667 pm. The two agree within about 0.4%, so the allowed orbit holds a whole number (2) of electron wavelengths, which supports Bohr's quantum condition.

questions.solution_md: $\lambda = 664.8$ pm (from the orbit) and $6.67 \times 10^{-10}$ m (de Broglie): they agree.

marking_scheme.step: Agreement: whole number of wavelengths in the orbit

questions.stem_md:
(a) State any three postulates of Bohr's theory of the atom. [3]

(b) The electron of an $\ce{Li^2+}$ ion ($Z = 3$) is in the third orbit. Calculate the radius of the orbit, and the energy of the electron, using $r_n = 52.9\,n^2/Z$ pm and $E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,Z^2/n^2$ J. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) The electron moves only in certain circular stationary orbits, in which it does not radiate; (ii) the angular momentum in an allowed orbit is a whole-number multiple of $h/2\pi$; (iii) energy is absorbed or emitted only when the electron jumps between orbits, as a photon with $\Delta E = h\nu$.

(b) $r_3 = \dfrac{52.9 \times 3^2}{3} = 158.7$ pm. $E_3 = -2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times \dfrac{3^2}{3^2} = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J (the same as the ground-state energy of hydrogen).

questions.solution_md: Three postulates; $r = 158.7$ pm; $E = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}$ J.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Give two merits of Bohr's model of the atom. [2]

(b) Explain why Bohr's model fails (i) for an atom with more than one electron, (ii) to account for the splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field and (iii) to agree with Heisenberg's principle. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) It explained the stability of the atom through stationary orbits in which no radiation occurs, and it explained the line spectrum of hydrogen and hydrogen-like ions, giving the radii, energies and wavelengths correctly.

(b) (i) It ignores the repulsion between electrons, so it gives wrong energies for helium and other many-electron atoms. (ii) It has only one quantum number, n, so it cannot account for the extra lines that appear when the source is placed in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) or an electric field (Stark effect). (iii) It treats the electron as a particle moving in a path of exactly known radius and speed, which Heisenberg's uncertainty principle shows is impossible, and it ignores the wave nature of the electron.

questions.solution_md: Two merits; three failures.

marking_scheme.step: (b)(iii) Conflict with uncertainty principle and wave nature

questions.stem_md: In a hydrogen discharge tube a line of wavelength 1875 nm, in the infrared, is recorded when the electron falls from n = 4. Using the Rydberg formula, the line belongs to the series ending on n = 3, the:

options.text_md: Paschen series
Lyman series
Balmer series
Brackett series

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{1875 \times 10^{-9}} = 5.33 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m}^{-1}$, and $1.097 \times 10^{7} \left(\dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{16}\right) = 5.33 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $n_1 = 3$, the Paschen series — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A flask of hydrogen atoms is excited so that electrons are raised to n = 5. Counting every possible route back to the ground state, the maximum number of different spectral lines emitted is:
questions.solution_md: Number of lines $= n(n-1)/2 = 5 \times 4/2 = 10$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The first line of the Balmer series of hydrogen has a wavelength of 656 nm. The wavelength of the Balmer line produced by the transition from n = 4 to n = 2 will be:

options.text_md: longer than 656 nm, because the energy gap is larger
equal to 656 nm, because both end on n = 2
shorter than 656 nm, because the gap is smaller
shorter than 656 nm, because the energy gap is larger

questions.solution_md: The 4 to 2 gap is larger than the 3 to 2 gap, so the photon has more energy and a shorter wavelength (486 nm) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The line of shortest wavelength in the Lyman series of hydrogen, called the series limit, is produced by the transition:

options.text_md: n = ∞ to n = 1
n = 2 to n = 1
n = ∞ to n = 2
n = 3 to n = 1

questions.solution_md: The largest gap in the series, from infinity to n = 1, gives the shortest wavelength — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following could Bohr’s model NOT explain?

options.text_md: the line spectrum of the hydrogen atom
the spectrum of the He⁺ ion
the stability of the hydrogen atom
the splitting of spectral lines when the source is placed in a magnetic field

questions.solution_md: Bohr’s single quantum number cannot account for the extra lines produced in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) — option (d). The other three are explained by the model.

questions.stem_md: Bohr’s formulas for energy give wrong results for the helium atom (two electrons) mainly because the model:

options.text_md: assumes that the nucleus has no charge
does not allow for the repulsion between the electrons
allows the electron to radiate energy continuously
uses a value of the Planck constant that is too small

questions.solution_md: Bohr’s theory treats a single electron attracted by the nucleus and ignores electron–electron repulsion — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Light is emitted when the electron of a hydrogen atom in a discharge tube falls from $n = 5$ to $n = 2$. Using $R_\text{H} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$, calculate the wavelength of this Balmer line in nm.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 1.097 \times 10^{7} \left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{25}\right) = 2.30 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{2.30 \times 10^{6}} = 4.34 \times 10^{-7}$ m; in nm: $4.34 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{9} = 434.1$, about 434 nm (violet).

questions.stem_md: In a spectrometer test of a hydrogen lamp, the third line of the Lyman series is recorded (the electron falls from $n = 4$ to $n = 1$). Calculate its wavelength in nm. ($R_\text{H} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 1.097 \times 10^{7} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{16}\right) = 1.028 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{1.028 \times 10^{7}} = 9.72 \times 10^{-8}$ m; in nm: $9.72 \times 10^{-8} \times 10^{9} = 97.2$ (ultraviolet).

questions.stem_md: The Balmer series of lines in the hydrogen spectrum arises when the electron falls to the level n = ___.
questions.solution_md: Balmer lines end on the level n = 2.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Bohr’s model can be used to calculate the radii and energies of the electron in He⁺ and Li²⁺ ions.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. These ions have only one electron, so r and E follow from the formulas with the appropriate Z.

questions.stem_md: Match each hydrogen spectral series with the lower level n₁ to which the electron falls.

options.text_md: Lyman
Balmer
Paschen
Brackett

questions.solution_md: Lyman → q (n = 1); Balmer → s (n = 2); Paschen → p (n = 3); Brackett → r (n = 4).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Lyman series of hydrogen lies in the visible region of the spectrum.

**Reason (R):** The lines of the Lyman series are produced when the electron falls to the level n = 2.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Lyman lines lie in the ultraviolet and end on n = 1, so both statements are false — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Bohr’s model gives correct wavelengths for the spectrum of the Li²⁺ ion.

**Reason (R):** The Li²⁺ ion contains more than one electron.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: Li²⁺ has a single electron, so the model applies. R is false: Li²⁺ has only one electron — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Write the Rydberg formula for the wave number of a line in the hydrogen spectrum, and name the series for which $n_1 = 1$ and for which $n_1 = 2$.

answer.model_answer_md: $\bar{\nu} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_\text{H}\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$, with $R_\text{H} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$ and $n_2 > n_1$. For $n_1 = 1$ the series is the Lyman series (ultraviolet); for $n_1 = 2$ it is the Balmer series (visible).

questions.solution_md: Rydberg formula; Lyman and Balmer.

questions.stem_md: Electrons in a sample of hydrogen are raised to the sixth level. How many different spectral lines can the sample emit, and how many of them are Lyman lines?

answer.model_answer_md: Number of lines $= \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$. Lyman lines end on $n = 1$, and can start from $n = 2, 3, 4, 5$ or $6$, so 5 of the 15 lines belong to the Lyman series.

questions.solution_md: $n(n-1)/2 = 15$ lines; 5 are Lyman lines.

questions.stem_md: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from the fourth level to the second. Name the series to which the line belongs, say in which region of the spectrum it lies, and write the relation between the energy change and the frequency.

answer.model_answer_md: The electron lands on n = 2, so the line belongs to the Balmer series, and it lies in the visible region (about 486 nm, blue-green). The energy difference between the two levels is emitted as one photon, ΔE = E₄ − E₂ = hν.

questions.solution_md: Balmer, visible; ΔE = hν.

questions.stem_md: The second line of the Paschen series of hydrogen arises when the electron falls from $n = 5$ to $n = 3$. Calculate its wavelength in nm, say in which region of the spectrum it lies and give its wave number. ($R_\text{H} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$)

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{25}\right) = 7.80 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m}^{-1}$ (the wave number). $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{7.80 \times 10^{5}} = 1.28 \times 10^{-6}$ m $\approx 1282$ nm, which is in the infrared region.

questions.solution_md: $\bar{\nu} = 7.80 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m}^{-1}$; $\lambda \approx 1282$ nm, infrared.

marking_scheme.step: Wave number from the Rydberg formula

questions.stem_md: List three defects of Bohr’s model of the atom.

answer.model_answer_md: It works only for one-electron species such as H, He⁺ and Li²⁺ and fails for atoms with more electrons. It cannot explain the fine splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) or in an electric field (Stark effect). It treats the electron as a particle in a definite orbit, ignoring its wave nature and contradicting Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle; it also gives no explanation of how atoms form chemical bonds.

questions.solution_md: Many-electron atoms; Zeeman and Stark effects; wave nature and uncertainty.

questions.stem_md: Name the first three series of the hydrogen spectrum, give the lower level n₁ of each and the region of the spectrum in which it lies.

answer.model_answer_md: Lyman series: n₁ = 1, ultraviolet region. Balmer series: n₁ = 2, visible region (with part in the near ultraviolet). Paschen series: n₁ = 3, infrared region.

questions.solution_md: Lyman 1 UV; Balmer 2 visible; Paschen 3 infrared.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the Rydberg formula for hydrogen and name the series, with the region of the spectrum, for $n_1 = 1, 2$ and $3$. [2]

(b) Calculate the longest and the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series. ($R_\text{H} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_\text{H}\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$ with $n_2 > n_1$. $n_1 = 1$: Lyman, ultraviolet; $n_1 = 2$: Balmer, visible; $n_1 = 3$: Paschen, infrared.

(b) Longest wavelength ($n_2 = 3$): $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = 1.52 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda = 656.3$ nm. Shortest wavelength (series limit, $n_2 = \infty$): $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1.097 \times 10^{7}}{4} = 2.74 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda = 364.6$ nm.

questions.solution_md: Rydberg formula; longest $656.3$ nm; shortest $364.6$ nm.

questions.stem_md: An electron beam in a microscope is accelerated so that the speed of its electrons rises from $1.0 \times 10^{6}$ to $4.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Its de Broglie wavelength changes by the factor:

options.text_md: four, so the wavelength becomes four times the original
one-half, so the wavelength becomes half the original
one-quarter, so the wavelength becomes one-quarter of the original
sixteen, so the wavelength becomes sixteen times the original

questions.solution_md: $\lambda = h/mv$ is inversely proportional to $v$, so a four-fold speed gives one-quarter of the wavelength — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A proton and an alpha particle (mass about four times that of the proton) move at the same speed. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the proton to that of the alpha particle is about:
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = h/mv$ with equal $v$ gives $\lambda_\text{p}/\lambda_\alpha = m_\alpha/m_\text{p} = 4$, so 4 : 1 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For an electron, $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq h/4\pi$. If the uncertainty in the position of the electron is reduced to half its value, the minimum uncertainty in its momentum:

options.text_md: becomes half as great
becomes twice as great
does not change
becomes four times as great

questions.solution_md: $\Delta p \geq h/(4\pi\,\Delta x)$ is inversely proportional to $\Delta x$, so halving $\Delta x$ doubles the minimum $\Delta p$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Wave behaviour is observed for a beam of electrons but never for a falling hailstone, because for the hailstone:

options.text_md: the mass is so large that λ = h/mv is far too small to detect
a hailstone has no mass
a hailstone cannot move at a measurable speed
the de Broglie relation applies only to charged particles

questions.solution_md: m is enormous compared with the electron’s, so λ = h/mv is immeasurably small — option (a). The relation applies to every moving object.

questions.stem_md: The idea that an electron in an atom travels in a circular path of exactly known radius and speed is rejected by modern theory because:

options.text_md: an electron has no mass and so cannot follow a path
the nucleus pushes the electron out of any circular path
the position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known exactly, so its path cannot be traced
the electron is a wave only when it is outside the atom

questions.solution_md: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle forbids exact simultaneous values of position and momentum, so a definite orbit has no meaning — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A tennis ball of mass $57\ \text{g}$ is served at $60\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength in units of $10^{-34}\ \text{m}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)

In a model of a hydrogen atom the position of the electron is fixed to within $2.0 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$. Calculate the minimum uncertainty in its speed, in units of $10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$)
questions.solution_md: $\Delta v = \dfrac{h}{4\pi m_\text{e} \Delta x} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{4 \times \pi \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.89 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$; in units of $10^{5}$: $2.89 \times 10^{5} / 10^{5} = 2.89$.

questions.stem_md: Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle states that the product of the uncertainty in position and the uncertainty in momentum is at least ___.
questions.solution_md: Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A tennis ball served at 60 m s⁻¹ has a de Broglie wavelength so small that its wave nature cannot be detected.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. For a ball, m is large, so λ = h/mv is about 10⁻³⁴ m, far smaller than anything measurable.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The uncertainty in the velocity of a dust grain of mass 1 μg is negligible, but for an electron it is large.

**Reason (R):** The product of mass and the uncertainty in position is far larger for the dust grain than for the electron, while h is the same.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Δv ≥ h/(4π m Δx): the very large mass makes Δv tiny for the grain, and the very small mass makes it large for the electron. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The de Broglie wavelength of an electron decreases when its speed increases.

**Reason (R):** Electrons carry a negative charge.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true since λ = h/mv. R is also true, but charge is unrelated to the wavelength relation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Write the de Broglie relation and explain each symbol. Why can we not observe the wave nature of a moving motorcycle?

answer.model_answer_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the matter wave, $h$ the Planck constant, $m$ the mass and $v$ the speed of the particle. For a motorcycle $m$ is very large, so $\lambda$ is extremely small (about $10^{-37}$ m) and cannot be detected.

questions.solution_md: λ = h/mv; large mass gives negligible wavelength.

questions.stem_md: State Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle and write its mathematical form, explaining the symbols.

answer.model_answer_md: It is impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both the position and the momentum of a moving microscopic particle such as an electron: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq \dfrac{h}{4\pi}$, where $\Delta x$ is the uncertainty in position, $\Delta p$ the uncertainty in momentum ($= m\,\Delta v$) and $h$ the Planck constant. The more exactly one is known, the less exactly the other can be.

questions.solution_md: Statement; Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π.

questions.stem_md: An electron in a television tube moves at $4.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength in pm, and say why its wave nature can be observed in crystals. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$)

answer.model_answer_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m_\text{e}v} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 4.0 \times 10^{6}} = 1.82 \times 10^{-10}$ m $= 182$ pm. This is of the order of the spacing between atoms in a crystal (about 100 to 300 pm), so a crystal can diffract the electron beam, as it diffracts X-rays.

questions.solution_md: $\lambda = 1.82 \times 10^{-10}$ m $= 182$ pm; comparable with atomic spacings.

marking_scheme.step: Comparable with atomic spacing, so diffraction

questions.stem_md: A dust grain of mass $1.0 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{kg}$ drifts in a still room with its speed known to within $1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the minimum uncertainty in its position and say whether the uncertainty principle has any practical effect on the grain. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$)

answer.model_answer_md: $\Delta x = \dfrac{h}{4\pi m\,\Delta v} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{4 \times \pi \times 1.0 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 5.27 \times 10^{-20}$ m. This is about $10^{-10}$ times the size of an atom, so it is utterly negligible: the principle has no practical effect on a particle of this size.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State de Broglie's relation, naming each quantity, and say what it implies for a moving particle. [2]

(b) Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of (i) an electron moving at $3.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and (ii) a bullet of mass $2.0\ \text{g}$ moving at $400\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, and comment on the two results. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\lambda = h/mv$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength, $h$ the Planck constant, $m$ the mass and $v$ the speed. Every moving particle has an associated matter wave, and its wavelength is inversely proportional to its momentum.

(b) (i) $\lambda = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 3.0 \times 10^{6}} = 2.42 \times 10^{-10}$ m. (ii) $\lambda = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{2.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 400} = 8.28 \times 10^{-34}$ m. The electron's wavelength is comparable with atomic dimensions and is detectable; the bullet's is far too small to detect.

questions.solution_md: Relation; electron $2.42 \times 10^{-10}$ m; bullet $8.28 \times 10^{-34}$ m.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and write its mathematical form. [2]

(b) The speed of an electron in a beam is known to within $1.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the minimum uncertainty in its position and comment on its size compared with an atom of diameter about $2 \times 10^{-10}$ m. ($h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$, $m_\text{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}$) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) It is impossible to know exactly and simultaneously both the position and the momentum of a microscopic particle: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq h/4\pi$.

(b) $\Delta x = \dfrac{h}{4\pi m_\text{e}\,\Delta v} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{4 \times \pi \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.0 \times 10^{5}} = 5.79 \times 10^{-10}$ m. This is about three times the diameter of an atom, so an electron whose speed is known this well cannot be said to be at any definite place inside the atom.

questions.solution_md: Statement and form; $\Delta x = 5.79 \times 10^{-10}$ m, larger than an atom.
